recommender_rubric.justification:
Scored against the rubric. The three options are distinct: each covers a different issue (maps, enforcement, funding and moratorium). They are conditional offers that match the opening package.

Feasibility (4): Each option rests on a real Indonesian constraint. Aggregated maps fit its domestic data law. A joint ASEAN panel avoids foreign jurisdiction. Tranche funding tied to results answers its limited fiscal capacity. The gap is that the panel has no compulsion power, which the text admits, citing Article 27 (no tribunal). Indonesia also has to accept it for that reason.

Tradeoff coverage (4): The risks are named. District data may be too coarse for Section 8 attribution. The panel may be toothless. The fund may pay out without cuts. Missing: Singapore's agribusiness lobby, the legally untested extraterritorial reach, and tenure disputes that overlap the concession registry. There is also no fallback if Indonesia refuses a panel.

Priority consistency (4): Funding only against verified reductions matches Singapore's red line. Keeping the Act on the books and Section 8 rights supports attribution. The weak point is that the attribution red line rests on coarse district data and a panel with no power. The text asserts that attribution is preserved but does not show how. The stated "serves equity/sovereignty/cost" tags are loose.

Counterpart consideration (4): Dropping Act application meets Indonesia's red line on foreign jurisdiction. Aggregated maps respect its data law. Funded transition and moratorium exemptions protect smallholders. The one weakness is that keeping the Act for non-cooperating firms may still irritate Indonesia, and the rationale puts the blame on Indonesian firms.

Strong arguments (4): It uses the strongest points in the briefs: Singapore cannot enforce on Indonesian soil, Indonesia's sovereignty and data constraints, Section 8 map-based presumption, and Article 27's lack of a tribunal. It does not use the S$2m fine cap or the Section 6 private suit as leverage.

transcript.position:
Singapore opens with a package built around one need: a way to say who caused the haze that still works after this episode ends. Between June and October 2015 our 24-hour PSI passed 300, schools closed, and regional losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars, so the cost of having no attribution is already measured. We therefore ask Indonesia's ministries to give full concession maps to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, because the ASEAN Agreement already requires each party's monitoring centre to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, and maps are what turn a hotspot into a named landholder. We also ask for a joint ASEAN panel to hear corporate attribution cases, because the Agreement's dispute clause offers only amicable consultation and no court or tribunal. In return we will not press for the Singapore Act to be applied to conduct inside Indonesia now. That is a real concession, since our Act reaches conduct abroad and presumes responsibility from land ownership, but we accept that Indonesia objects to its extraterritorial reach and that a panel gives Jakarta a seat at the table.

The most damaging objection is sovereignty: Indonesia will say that handing over maps and accepting outside review violates its data law and its right to use its own resources. We answer that the same Agreement that protects that right also bars damage to other states, and that the maps go to a regional ASEAN body, not to Singapore's courts. Our offer on money is conditional. We will help direct partial donor funding for peatland transition and will back a full peatland moratorium with no exemptions, but we will not fund transition unless measurable reductions in hotspots and PSI exposure are verified with our satellite monitoring. If Indonesia accepts the maps and the panel, we can discuss how fast the funding and the moratorium's coverage are phased in, but not whether an attribution mechanism exists.

transcript.position: Indonesia is ready to act on the haze, but it will do so through its own courts, its own agencies and a funded transition. The 2015 haze ran from June to October and pushed Singapore's PSI past 300, so we accept that the harm is real and that prevention is urgent. However, the ASEAN Agreement already fixes the remedy: Article 27 settles disputes by consultation, and Article 3(1) keeps each party's sovereign right over its own resources. Singapore's Act reaches conduct abroad and presumes liability from concession maps. Our enforcement therefore stays with Indonesian courts, and we will not release parcel-level maps that would hand a foreign court its evidence. In return we offer a moratorium with limited exemptions, because that is our fastest and cheapest lever. We can make it binding through provincial administrations before the El Nino dry season, which has a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the northern winter. The most damaging objection is that Indonesian courts alone will not deter burning. We answer that Article 9 already obliges us to control open burning, and the Peatland Restoration Agency set up under Presidential Regulation 1/2016 gives us a domestic enforcement body with a clear mandate. Prevention only works for smallholders if it is funded, because a ban without alternatives pushes them back to fire. We therefore ask donors, who gain the most from clearer air, to fund the transition in full. If Singapore and donors accept that, we can discuss sharing district-level aggregated data under Article 8(1) at a later stage, but not in exchange for nothing.

recommender_rubric.justification:
Feasibility (4): Option 1 matches Indonesia's round-3 offer almost exactly: full maps, a referral route, report-back, and the Act dropped. Option 3 matches terms both sides already accepted, namely tranches released against satellite-verified reductions. Option 2 is weaker. It rests on Indonesia refusing parcel maps, which Indonesia has already moved past. The panel it keeps is one Indonesia has rejected as a red line.

Tradeoff coverage (3): The options cover maps, enforcement and funding. The moratorium is only a concession inside option 3. The recommendation does not address Indonesia's request to flag parcels in unresolved tenure disputes. It also does not address how attribution works if Indonesian courts are slow or lenient, beyond naming that as a risk. The agribusiness lobby and the legal uncertainty of extraterritorial prosecution get only a passing mention.

Priority consistency (3): Option 1 keeps maps and attribution, which serves Singapore's first red line. Option 3 keeps the red line on funding without measurable reductions. Giving up the panel, the only body that could decide responsibility, leaves attribution resting on Indonesian referral and report-back. That is a risk to the red line, and the text admits the risk. The rationale also says the panel is "the only remaining gap". The headline contradicts the options by saying "Drop … a joint panel to get full maps", while option 2 holds the panel.

Counterpart consideration (4): The recommendation takes Indonesia's sovereignty red line, its funded-transition need and its courts-only enforcement seriously. It adopts the referral route and report-back that Indonesia proposed. It does not engage the tenure-dispute flagging request or Indonesia's fiscal limits. The rationale's line that Indonesia and donors should bear prevention costs sits oddly with those limits.

scores.justification: It builds on an existing treaty duty (Article 8(1)) and offers to hold its Act in reserve. But a joint ASEAN panel has no basis in the 2002 Agreement, which has no tribunal under Article 27. It does not say who would set up, staff or fund the panel. Full maps are also the item Indonesia has refused so far.

It cites exact figures (S$2 million cap, section 5(5), section 8, Article 8(1)). Funding is only tied to 'measurable reductions in hotspots and PSI days', with no amounts, thresholds, donor shares or schedule. The panel's powers and procedures are left for later discussion.

It admits 'Singapore cannot compel enforcement on Indonesian soil'. It also accepts that conditional funding adds cost for Singapore and donors, and it gives up direct use of the Act. It does not admit that full maps and a no-exemption moratorium cost Indonesia, including smallholders and tenure disputes. It treats the S$2 million cap as limiting Indonesia's exposure while ignoring civil suits under section 6.

This is the opening round. The package, concessions and red lines match its own stated needs: attribution first, funding only with verified results. The concessions are conditioned and explained, and nothing contradicts itself.

It anticipates the sovereignty objection and answers it with Article 3(1). It frames maps as going to a regional body, not to Singapore. It says a joint panel answers Indonesia's objection to extraterritorial reach better than the Act. It does not address smallholder livelihoods or tenure disputes.

judgments.summary: Singapore proposes that Indonesia give full concession maps to the regional haze monitoring system and that a joint ASEAN panel hear attribution cases. Singapore would hold its own law in reserve. It also asks for a full peatland moratorium with no exemptions. It would back a partial donor fund released only against measured falls in hotspots and bad-air days. The argument is clear and well sourced and is built around attribution. The panel and the funding terms are thin and the costs to Indonesia are underplayed.

The late-2015 moratorium and the January 2016 Peatland Restoration Agency show a full no-exemption moratorium is 'the direction already set'. The background supports only that they exist, not that exemptions are excluded.

scores.justification: The Peatland Restoration Agency already exists and Indonesian courts already exist. District-level data can be shared quickly. But it demands a full donor fund without naming donors or amounts. Courts-only enforcement may not meet Singapore's attribution need, and the district data may not identify owners.

It names a clear data tier (district-level, not parcel-level) and a clear enforcement forum. It also cites the S$100,000 per day fine and the BRG regulation. It gives no fund size, no list of exemptions, no timetable and no description of how Indonesian courts would act on fires.

It concedes that attribution without maps is its 'most damaging objection' and that Section 8 relies on maps. It also says Indonesia cannot carry the cost alone. It does not say what district-only data and courts-only enforcement cost Singapore, namely weaker attribution and no outside check on enforcement. It does not mention the risk of exemptions for large plantations.

This is the opening round. It is coherent with its stated red lines on foreign jurisdiction and smallholders. Its concessions on district-level maps and partial exemptions are explicitly conditional on courts-only enforcement and full funding. It does not reverse itself.

It engages the Singapore Act directly, citing sections 4, 5(2)(a) and 8. It takes up the likely attribution argument and answers with the limited scope of Article 8(1). It does not address the joint panel idea, which gets no reply.

judgments.summary: Indonesia proposes that Indonesian courts and the government handle all enforcement, with the Peatland Restoration Agency running the moratorium. It would share concession data only at district level and keep parcel-level maps at home. It would accept a moratorium with targeted exemptions if donors fully fund the transition. The argument is firm on sovereignty and smallholders and responds to the Singapore Act. Several factual supports are missing, and it does not explain how attribution would work without parcel maps.

A joint panel has no legal basis in the 2002 Agreement. Neither side says whether it needs a treaty change, or how its rulings would be enforced inside Indonesia.
The size, donors and governance of the transition fund. Neither side says who else besides Singapore would pay, and how results would be verified if the maps dispute is unresolved.
The effect of moratorium exemptions on large plantation holders versus smallholders. Neither side separates these groups or says who bears compensation for existing permits.

recommender_rubric.justification: Feasibility (4): Options 1 and 2 track what Indonesia offered in Round 3 (per-hotspot ownership findings reported to ASEAN, smallholder exemptions, drought-adjusted satellite-verified tranches). Option 3 is a walk-away fallback that Singapore can do alone. Weaknesses: the "Singapore-visible review of unexplained inaction" is vague, and Indonesia may see it as a foreign check. Tradeoff coverage (3): It covers attribution against sovereignty, cost against results, and the risk of no deal. It leaves out section 6 private claims as a sticking point in the live options, Singapore's fixed share and shortfall protection, and how to identify smallholders. It also leaves out the disputed-tenure risk of wrongful attribution and the dry-season timing. Priority consistency (3): The attribution red line and the results-linked funding are kept, and the walk-away option protects both. But the headline says "independent attribution check" while option 1 drops the panel for a prosecutor check with only a weak review. That is hard to square with Singapore's red line and its aim of holding corporate actors accountable. The recommendation also concedes the full moratorium without getting anything in return that is firm. Counterpart consideration (4): It accepts Indonesian courts first, smallholder exemptions and district data, and it respects the sovereignty and smallholder concerns. It does not address Indonesia's objection that panel findings would feed section 6 suits, and option 3 uses section 6 as leverage, which crosses Indonesia's stated red line. Strong arguments (3): It uses the debate's main convergence points, namely district data, the full fund, drought adjustment and reporting. It does not use the strongest Singapore arguments, such as the panel being attribution-only, the registry-based owner names or the exclusion of disputed parcels. The rationale also asserts that operators "cause the haze" and that they and donors should bear the cost, which is a moral claim, not a cited argument. transcript.position:
Singapore asks for a settlement that makes the next dry season measurably different from 2015, when the 24-hour PSI passed 300, schools closed and regional losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars [Background]. We propose four things. First, Indonesia's agriculture and forestry authorities send plantation concession maps in full to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, because without maps nobody can say whose land is burning. Second, offenders face a Singapore-law track for companies that cause haze in Singapore, with Indonesian courts and agencies free to act first. Third, the new peatland moratorium applies to all concessions with no exemptions. Fourth, donors fund a partial transition package that releases money only against measured fire and haze reductions.

The strongest objection is sovereignty, and we answer it with the treaty Indonesia has signed. Article 3(1) of the ASEAN haze agreement protects the right to exploit resources but pairs it with a duty not to damage other states, and Article 8(1) already obliges each party to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre [S1]. Sharing maps is therefore an extension of an existing duty and not a new surrender. Article 27 offers only consultation, with no court or tribunal, so the treaty alone cannot produce attribution [S1]. Our Act is modest by comparison: the fine is up to S$100,000 per day but the aggregate is capped at S$2 million, which is reached after just 20 days of haze, so it cannot be a ruinous burden on honest firms [S2 section 5(2)(a) and 5(5)]. Section 8 presumes the landholder caused the fire, and ownership can be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government, so maps are what make the system work and also what lets innocent landholders clear their names [S2]. We cannot compel enforcement inside Indonesia and we say so openly, which is why the attribution route runs through shared maps and not through Singapore reaching into Indonesian territory.

We can move, but only in return for movement. If Indonesia accepts full map sharing with the ASEAN monitoring system, Singapore can accept that Indonesian courts lead on enforcement for fires on Indonesian land, with a joint ASEAN panel reviewing attribution. If Indonesia accepts a moratorium with no exemptions, Singapore can direct regional development and donor funding to the transition, scaled to verified reductions. We will not sign any settlement that has no attribution mechanism, because 2015 would then repeat with no way to name who is responsible. We will not fund a transition without measurable reductions, because unconditional money would pay for the same burning cycle.

key_claims.claim: Sharing concession maps extends a duty Indonesia already accepted and is what makes attribution possible.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1] requires each party's monitoring centre to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, and [S2] section 8 allows ownership to be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government.

key_claims.claim: The treaty alone cannot settle who is responsible, so a binding attribution mechanism is needed.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 limits dispute settlement to amicable consultation or negotiation with no court or tribunal, while the 2015 episode pushed PSI above 300 over June to October [Background].

key_claims.claim: Singapore's Act is proportionate and does not threaten honest operators.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 5(2)(a) sets fines up to S$100,000 per day and section 5(5) caps the aggregate at S$2 million, which is reached after 20 days of haze.

key_claims.claim: Corporate accountability reaches landholders who cause haze in Singapore, wherever they operate.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 4 extends the Act to conduct outside Singapore, and section 6 lets anyone in Singapore who suffers injury, property damage or economic loss sue.

concessions: If Indonesia accepts full map sharing, Singapore can let Indonesian courts lead on fires on Indonesian land with a joint ASEAN panel reviewing attribution.
If Indonesia accepts a moratorium with no exemptions, Singapore can direct donor funding to a partial transition package.
Funding is released in tranches only as measured reductions in fires and haze are verified.
red_lines: No settlement without an attribution mechanism, because without it the dry-season cycle that pushed PSI above 300 in 2015 has no named responsible party.
No transition funding without measurable reductions, because unconditional money would finance the same burning.

transcript.position:
Indonesia accepts that the 2015 haze, with Singapore's PSI above 300 between June and October, demands action, and we are acting through a peatland moratorium and a Peatland Restoration Agency set up in January 2016. However, the fix must be built on the 2002 ASEAN agreement, which keeps each party's sovereign right over its own resources and says disputes are settled by consultation, not by any court. Our proposal is that Indonesian courts and the Indonesian government alone enforce against fires on Indonesian soil. Singapore's 2014 Act reaches conduct abroad and presumes liability from concession maps supplied by a foreign government, so releasing parcel-level maps would hand a foreign court the evidence to rule on acts on our territory. That would cost us the sovereign enforcement authority that our whole fire-control effort rests on. Our data law also bars parcel-level disclosure, and unresolved tenure disputes overlap the registry, so publishing raw maps would wrongly expose innocent smallholders to claims. We will keep concession maps withheld for now, while continuing to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre as the agreement requires.

The most damaging objection is that Indonesia is offering words while the smoke returns, since El Nino has a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter. Our answer is that fires are put out by funded alternatives on the ground, not by foreign fines, because the Singapore Act's aggregate cap is only S$2 million, small beside losses in the tens of billions of dollars. In return for a full donor fund for transition, which lets provincial administrations pay smallholders not to burn and rewet peat, we will accept a moratorium with partial exemptions rather than blanket exemptions. This is a real concession on peatland rules, offered only if funding is committed and enforcement stays with Indonesian courts. We cannot accept any restriction that lands on smallholders without funded alternatives, because it would strip livelihoods from farmers during the planting window and we cannot finance that alone.

key_claims.claim: The ASEAN haze agreement gives no court or tribunal power, so foreign adjudication of acts on Indonesian soil has no treaty basis.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 says disputes are settled amicably by consultation or negotiation, and Article 3(1) preserves each party's sovereign right to exploit its own resources, so Indonesian-only enforcement fits what ASEAN states already agreed.

key_claims.claim: Handing over parcel-level concession maps would feed liability claims in a foreign court, which is why Indonesia withholds them.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 8 presumes that whoever owns or occupies land where a fire burns caused the haze and allows ownership to be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government, while section 4 extends the Act to conduct outside Singapore.

key_claims.claim: Foreign fines are too small to prevent fires, whereas funded transition does, so money should go to alternatives rather than penalties.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 5(5) caps the aggregate fine at S$2 million, against regional losses in the tens of billions of dollars from the 2015 episode [Background].

key_claims.claim: The risk is immediate, so funding must be in place before the next burning season.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] The ENSO Diagnostic Discussion of 13 August 2015 gave a greater than 90% chance that El Nino lasts through the 2015-16 northern winter, and the Peatland Restoration Agency was only established in January 2016.

key_claims.claim: Indonesia already meets its data-sharing duty through monitoring data rather than parcel maps.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1) requires each party's monitoring centre to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, and it does not require parcel-level concession maps.

concessions: Conditional on a full donor fund and courts-only enforcement, Indonesia will accept a moratorium with partial exemptions instead of blanket exemptions for existing concessions.
Indonesia will keep sending fire and haze monitoring data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre under Article 8(1) of the 2002 agreement.
Indonesia is open to discussing less sensitive aggregated data later, but only if the funding and enforcement terms are secured first.
red_lines: No foreign jurisdiction over acts on Indonesian soil: a foreign court ruling on Indonesian fires would set a precedent and undercut the sole enforcement authority of Indonesian authorities.
No restriction that falls on smallholders without funded alternatives: unfunded limits would remove livelihoods through the planting window, and Indonesia cannot finance the transition alone.

scores.justification: Tranche-based funding tied to verified reductions and a staged courts-first approach are workable. But full map sharing plus a Singapore-law track runs straight into Indonesia's stated data-law and sovereignty limits, and no one is named to verify the reductions or to fund the package.

It gives concrete figures (S$100,000 per day, S$2 million cap, 20 days to reach the cap) and cites specific sections. The funding package has no amount, tranche schedule or verification body, and the joint panel's design is not described.

It admits 'We cannot compel enforcement inside Indonesia' and offers to let Indonesian courts lead. It never admits that full maps expose Indonesian landholders, including smallholders, to claims. It calls the Act modest while ignoring the uncapped civil suits under s6, which its own claim cites.

The four-part opening matches the package (full maps, Singapore Act applied, no-exemption moratorium, partial fund). The conditional offer to let Indonesian courts lead is framed as a concession, not a reversal. Offering a courts-lead arrangement while the package says Singapore Act applied is a small tension.

This is an opening round, but it anticipates the 'strongest objection is sovereignty' and answers it with Articles 3(1), 8(1) and 27. It does not engage the data-law or tenure-overlap concerns that Indonesia raises.

judgments.summary: Singapore proposes full sharing of concession maps with the ASEAN monitoring system, a Singapore-law track for firms causing haze (with Indonesian courts free to act first), a moratorium with no exemptions, and donor money released in tranches against verified fire and haze cuts. It argues that map sharing extends an existing treaty duty and that its fines are modest. It offers to let Indonesian courts lead, with an ASEAN panel reviewing attribution, if Indonesia shares maps. Its red lines are no deal without a way to name those responsible and no money without measured reductions. The argument is specific and clear, but it stretches Article 8(1), which covers fire and haze data, to cover parcel maps. It also downplays uncapped civil liability and the exposure of innocent landholders.
unsupported_claims: 'The treaty Indonesia has signed': neither the scenario nor [S1] lists which states are parties or says Indonesia ratified.
Section 8 lets innocent landholders clear their names: [S2] s8 only says ownership can be proved from foreign-government maps, and nothing in the source describes a defence for innocent holders.
Article 8(1) covers concession maps, so sharing maps is an extension of an existing duty: [S1] Article 8(1) covers fire and haze data only.

scores.justification: Courts-only enforcement and keeping the existing data feed are easy to carry out. judgments.summary: Indonesia proposes that Indonesian courts and the government alone enforce against fires on Indonesian soil, that concession maps stay withheld while fire and haze monitoring data keeps flowing to the ASEAN centre, and that the moratorium allows partial exemptions. It argues that foreign fines are too small to stop fires and that releasing parcel-level maps would hand a foreign court evidence to rule on acts on its territory. transcript.position: Singapore opens with a package built around one need: a way to say which company's land burned, that still works after this episode ends. The 2015 fires pushed the 24-hour PSI past 300 and closed schools, so a repeat in the next dry season is a real risk, and without concession maps nobody can prove who owns burning land. We therefore ask Indonesia to give full concession maps to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, and we answer the sovereignty objection directly: the 2002 Agreement already requires each party's monitoring centre to pass fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, and it keeps the right to use resources only alongside a duty not to harm neighbours. Maps shared with a regional body, not with Singapore's courts alone, are the same kind of data sharing Indonesia has already accepted in principle. In return we will not push for Singapore's Act to be the enforcing instrument this round. We propose a joint ASEAN panel instead, because the Agreement offers only amicable consultation and no tribunal, and a panel fills that gap without Singapore claiming to compel anything inside Indonesia. The strongest objection to this package is that it hands Singapore a tool against Indonesian-linked firms. Our answer is that the Act's daily fine of up to S$100,000 is capped at S$2 million in total, so it is a deterrent signal and not a punitive weapon, and a joint panel puts Indonesia at the table. On peat, we want the moratorium to apply with no exemptions, since exempting existing permits leaves the already-drained land that burns outside the rule. On money, we will contribute to a partial donor fund, but only with measurable reductions in hotspots as the release condition, because we will not pay for a transition that cannot show results. We are open to movement on funding size and on moratorium exemptions if maps and a working attribution mechanism are secured.

key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 8 presumes that an entity owning or occupying land where a fire burns caused the haze, and allows ownership to be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government, so without maps this presumption cannot operate.

transcript.position: Indonesia accepts that the 2015 haze was a regional emergency and is ready to act, but the fires are on Indonesian soil, so enforcement must stay with Indonesian courts and agencies. The 2002 ASEAN agreement already says parties keep the sovereign right to use their own resources, and it settles disputes by consultation, with no court at all. Singapore's 2014 Act reaches conduct abroad, fines up to S$100,000 a day and presumes guilt from land ownership proved by maps a foreign government supplies. That is why we cannot accept a foreign statute applied here, and why we will not hand over parcel-level concession maps. Our data law restricts that disclosure, and the registry overlaps unresolved tenure disputes, so raw maps would wrongly name smallholders as culprits. In return we offer district-level aggregated concession data to the ASEAN monitoring system, which meets the agreement's duty to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre. We also offer a moratorium with limited exemptions, run through the Peatland Restoration Agency created in January 2016 and the provincial administrations.\n\nThe strongest objection we expect is that Indonesian courts alone will not deter burning and that withheld maps leave Singapore blind. Our answer is that district data lets the monitoring system place hotspots against fires, while Indonesian prosecution avoids a clash with our law. Singapore's own Act caps the total fine at S$2 million, so its deterrent is small compared with funded restoration. The moratorium falls on smallholders at the start of the planting window, so we can only impose it if donors fund alternatives. With El Nino over 90% likely to last through the 2015-16 winter, delay is costly for everyone, so we ask for a full donor fund now. If the other side accepts Indonesian enforcement and full funding, we can move on map detail and moratorium scope.

transcript.position:
We have moved on three of four issues since last round: we now accept partial exemptions in the moratorium and a full donor fund, and we keep the joint panel in place of our own Act, but we hold on full concession maps to the regional monitoring system because that is where attribution lives. Indonesia answered that its fears are foreign jurisdiction and unfunded smallholders, and we meet both. Its strongest point was that district data satisfies the treaty duty. That is true of Article 8(1) of the 2002 Agreement, which only requires fire and haze data to reach the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, but it does not show who owns burning land, and section 8 of our Act, the only ownership presumption on the table, runs on ownership proved from maps. Therefore district totals cannot attribute a fire to a company, and a joint panel or an Indonesian court would have nothing to decide on. We concede that Article 8(1) does not itself compel map sharing, so we are asking for it as a bargained term, not a treaty right.

To answer the smallholder risk, we propose that maps go only to the regional monitoring system and not to Singapore's courts, and that parcels on disputed tenure be flagged and excluded until the Peatland Restoration Agency and provincial administrations clear them, so smallholders are not wrongly named. In return for that, Singapore will drop its Act as the enforcement route, which Indonesia calls its first red line, and accept a joint panel that complements Indonesian courts, because Article 27 provides no tribunal at all. We will also support a full donor fund, but money is released in tranches against measured falls in hotspots, because we will not fund a transition without measurable reductions. We also state openly that section 6 of our Act lets injured people sue for losses without the S$2 million cap, and we are ready to discuss how that interacts with the panel. Timing matters too: the moratorium should bite on each area only once its funded alternatives arrive, so farmers are not left without income in the planting window, and El Nino is over 90% likely to last through the 2015-16 winter, so delay serves no one. If Indonesia accepts full maps with the tenure-clearing safeguard, we give it the enforcement and funding terms it asked for.

Singapore's strongest point is that without maps nobody can prove whose land burned. That is fair, but a blanket parcel release is not the only fix. Our domestic data law restricts parcel-level disclosure and the registry overlaps unresolved tenure disputes, so raw maps would wrongly name smallholders. Instead, the Peatland Restoration Agency, created in January 2016, and the provincial administrations will verify ownership for each hotspot fire inside Indonesia, and Indonesian courts will prosecute on that evidence. District data tells the monitoring system where fires cluster, which is the fire and haze data Article 8(1) of the 2002 Agreement requires us to send to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre. judgments.summary: Indonesia offers district-level aggregated data, enforcement kept in Indonesian courts, a moratorium with partial exemptions run through the restoration agency, and a full donor fund. scores.justification: Phasing each province's moratorium in as its tranche is paid, and releasing tranches against ASEAN hotspot counts, can be carried out. Gives clear mechanics: moratorium starts by province at tranche disbursement, money is released against ASEAN hotspot counts, and the Peatland Restoration Agency and provinces verify ownership per hotspot fire and pass evidence to Indonesian courts. Moves from partial exemptions to a full moratorium with no exemptions and accepts release against hotspot reductions, and states both. These are explained concessions. judgments.summary: Indonesia moves to accept a full moratorium with no exemptions and money released against measured hotspot falls, and starts each province's moratorium only when its funding arrives. It keeps district-level data, Indonesian courts only and a full fund. Its answer to the attribution problem is that Indonesian agencies verify who owns land for each hotspot fire and give the evidence to Indonesian courts. unaddressed_tradeoffs: Neither side says who pays for a full donor fund or how large it is, or what happens if donors will not fund it in full.

Our red lines (an attribution mechanism, and no funding without measurable reductions) point to trading away our Act for flagged-parcel maps and tranche-based funding. The crisis does not pull sharply apart on any single priority, so this is the baseline package.

recommender_rubric.justification: Feasibility (4): Option 1 mirrors Singapore's own Round 2 offer, with maps to the HMS only, flagged tenure parcels, tranche funding and a joint panel alongside Indonesian courts. It is workable. Option 3 is a hold-and-review fallback with plausible mechanics. Option 2 is fine, though it keeps section 6 "in reserve", which is a provocative step against Indonesia's red line. Tradeoff coverage (3): it covers the maps-versus-sovereignty tension, funding conditionality, and under-reporting and stall risks. It barely addresses moratorium timing, with phasing by province tied to tranches, which Indonesia raised in round 2. It does not address the section 6 uncapped civil route as a negotiating issue. The rationale also says the crisis "does not pull sharply apart", which is wrong given the maps/sovereignty conflict. It also blames the haze on operators and Indonesia, and wording like "serves equity/cost" reads as generic labelling. Priority consistency (4): it holds both red lines, attribution and no funding without measurable reductions. Option 2 strains the attribution red line, and the recommendation admits this. Option 3 keeps attribution through a published evidence process that the panel can review. Counterpart consideration (4): it engages Indonesia's smallholder and tenure concerns through the flagged parcels and tranche phasing. It also offers Indonesian courts alongside the panel. However, it does not tie the moratorium start to disbursement, and it holds section 6 in reserve, which cuts against Indonesia's red line on foreign jurisdiction. Strong arguments (3): it draws on the key point that district data cannot attribute ownership under section 8, and on tranches against hotspots. It omits the strongest debate points: that Indonesia's per-case verification can serve as attribution, that the fine cap is small, and the El Niño urgency. Options are 3 and genuinely distinct, since they are conditioned on different Indonesian stances, though they are all variants on the same maps/funding axis.

transcript.position:
Singapore opens by asking for a settlement that makes the next haze episode both preventable and provable. Our 24-hour PSI passed 300 in 2015, schools closed, and regional losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars, so a deal that repeats the 2002 ASEAN Agreement cannot be enough. That Agreement leaves disputes to consultation with no court or tribunal, and without concession maps nobody can say which company's land burned. We therefore propose that Indonesia give full concession maps to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, that a joint ASEAN panel hear attribution and enforcement cases rather than leaving them to either state alone, that the peatland moratorium apply without exemptions, and that donors fund a partial transition programme whose payments are released only against measured reductions in hotspots and PSI days.

We expect Indonesia to object that sharing maps and accepting a panel violates its sovereignty. We answer that the Agreement itself already recognises sovereign use of resources together with a duty not to damage other states, and already obliges each party to pass fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, so a regional panel is a step within ASEAN rather than outside it. In return for accepting this, Singapore will not press for application of its own Act against Indonesian operators, even though the Act extends to conduct abroad and presumes liability for the owner of burning land. Singapore will also direct donor funding to the transition, because Indonesia carries the cost of restoration and has the strongest claim to help with it. Funding stays conditional on measurable reductions, because we cannot justify spending public money without results.

key_claims.claim: Without concession maps no attribution mechanism can work, and the 2015 episode shows the cost: PSI above 300 and regional losses in the tens of billions of dollars.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] The 2015 haze pushed Singapore's 24-hour PSI past 300 and cost the region tens of billions of dollars, and [S2] section 8 shows ownership can be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government, so maps are what turn a fire into a named responsible party.

key_claims.claim: A joint ASEAN panel fills a gap that the 2002 Agreement leaves open, and it respects sovereignty better than Singapore applying its own Act in Indonesia.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 settles disputes by consultation or negotiation with no court or tribunal, while [S1] Article 3(1) keeps each party's sovereign right to use its resources, so a regional panel gives a remedy without foreign courts reaching into Indonesia.

key_claims.claim: Singapore's own Act is a moderate lever, so giving up its use in this deal is a real but affordable concession that Indonesia should value.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 5(2)(a) allows fines of up to S$100,000 per day of haze, capped at S$2 million in aggregate by section 5(5), and section 4 extends the Act to conduct outside Singapore, which is the reach Indonesia objected to in 2015.

key_claims.claim: Data sharing is already an agreed duty, so full maps ask for implementation, not for a new obligation.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1) requires each party's monitoring centre to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, and the Agreement has been in force since 25 November 2003.

concessions: Singapore will not insist that its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act be applied against Indonesian operators, provided the joint ASEAN panel can use the shared maps to attribute fires to concession holders.
Singapore will channel donor funding to a partial transition programme, provided payments are tied to measured reductions in hotspots and PSI days.
red_lines: No settlement without a working attribution mechanism: without maps and a body able to name responsible concession holders, the dry-season cycle that pushed PSI past 300 in 2015 will repeat unchallenged.
No transition funding without measurable reductions: unconditional payments cannot be justified to Singapore taxpayers and give Indonesia no incentive to cut fires.

transcript.position: Indonesia accepts that the 2015 haze, when Singapore's 24-hour PSI passed 300 between June and October, must not happen again, and we will act against it ourselves. However, the right tool is Indonesian enforcement, not a foreign statute. The ASEAN Agreement that both countries signed keeps each party's sovereign right to use its own resources (Article 3(1)) and settles disputes by consultation, with no court or tribunal (Article 27). Singapore's Act reaches conduct outside Singapore (section 4), lets private claimants sue (section 6), and presumes that a landowner caused the haze using maps supplied by a foreign government (section 8). Therefore our enforcement must stay with Indonesian courts, and we ask Singapore to accept that. The strongest objection to this is that Indonesian enforcement has not stopped the fires. We answer that the Peatland Restoration Agency, created in January 2016 under Presidential Regulation 1/2016, and a moratorium now give us the tools to do so. A Singaporean fine cap of S$2 million in aggregate (section 5(5)) would also do little against losses in the tens of billions of dollars, so the Act adds a precedent we cannot accept but little real deterrence.\n\nIn return for Singapore accepting Indonesian courts, we offer movement where it costs us least. First, we can share concession information aggregated by district through the ASEAN data channel, which is consistent with the duty to send fire and haze data at agreed intervals (Article 8(1)). Parcel-level maps stay home because domestic data law restricts them and tenure disputes overlap the registry. Second, we can apply a moratorium with partial exemptions, run by provincial administrations in phases. This is conditional on a fully funded donor transition fund, because El Nino conditions with a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the northern winter mean restrictions would otherwise land on smallholders at the start of the planting window with no alternative income. We cannot fund this alone. Whoever wants a tighter moratorium and more data should help pay for it.

key_claims.claim: Enforcement against Indonesian-soil acts must stay with Indonesian courts, because the regional treaty itself preserves sovereignty and creates no external tribunal.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 3(1) keeps each party's sovereign right to exploit its own resources and Article 27 settles disputes by consultation with no court or tribunal, so a foreign statute going beyond that would override what both countries signed in 2002.

key_claims.claim: Singapore's Act is a jurisdiction precedent for us rather than an effective deterrent, so accepting it would cost much and gain little.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 5(5) caps the aggregate fine at S$2 million while [Background] regional losses from the 2015 haze ran into the tens of billions of dollars, yet section 4 extends the Act to conduct outside Singapore and section 6 opens civil suits to anyone in Singapore.

key_claims.claim: Parcel-level concession maps cannot be released, but district-level data meets the treaty's monitoring duty and still serves Singapore's need to trace fires.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1) requires fire and haze data to be sent to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, which district-level aggregates satisfy, while [S2] section 8 shows Singapore wants parcel maps mainly to presume liability against landowners, which is the foreign-jurisdiction use we reject.

key_claims.claim: A moratorium can only be phased in with funded alternatives for smallholders, and the timing is dangerous.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] El Nino conditions carry a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter (ENSO Diagnostic Discussion, 13 August 2015), so fire risk is highest just when a restriction would take away smallholders' land-clearing options, and [S1] Article 9 requires us to prevent land clearing by fire, which is only workable if there is a funded substitute.

concessions: Conditional on Indonesian courts handling enforcement, Indonesia will share concession data aggregated by district through the ASEAN channel.
Conditional on a fully funded donor transition fund, Indonesia will apply a moratorium with only partial exemptions, phased by provincial administrations, rather than exempting all existing permits.
red_lines: No foreign jurisdiction over acts on Indonesian soil: applying Singapore's Act, with its reach under section 4 and civil liability under section 6, would set a precedent of foreign courts ruling on Indonesian land.
No restriction that falls on smallholders without funded alternatives: with El Nino risk through the northern winter, an unfunded ban would remove livelihoods through the planting window.

transcript.position: We have moved on two issues since last round: Singapore now accepts a moratorium with partial exemptions and will back a fully funded donor transition, in return for full concession maps held under restricted access and a joint ASEAN panel instead of Singapore's own Act. Indonesia's strongest point is that a fine cap of S$2 million in aggregate under section 5(5) does little against losses in the tens of billions of dollars, and that our Act sets a jurisdiction precedent. We agree the cap is small, and that is exactly why we will drop the Act: what deters is being named, not the fine, so attribution matters more to us than punishment. We also accept the correction that Article 8(1) covers fire and haze data and not concession maps, and that Article 27 shows the treaty has no tribunal. The maps and the panel are therefore new commitments, and we pay for them. Indonesia says its main needs are enforcement staying in Indonesian hands and a funded transition. Singapore offers the second in full: if Indonesia accepts parcel-level maps lodged with the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System and a joint ASEAN panel, we will accept partial exemptions and will direct donors toward a full transition fund. Because we cannot spend public money without results, the fund is released in tranches against verified falls in hotspots and PSI days, measured from satellite monitoring that Singapore already operates and checked against data that Indonesia's own centre sends under Article 8(1). This answers the question of who measures. The most damaging objection to our plan is that parcel maps allow the section 8 presumption against Indonesian landowners. We answer it by dropping the Act from this deal, and by limiting map access to the panel's verified staff, so maps cannot be used in Singapore courts. Section 6 private suits remain open by law and Singapore cannot waive them for private claimants, but with the panel as the forum for attribution, the fund tied to results, and the Act set aside for state enforcement, Indonesia gets a regional process in place of a foreign one. Without a working attribution mechanism we cannot sign, because a fire that cannot be tied to a concession holder will recur in the next dry season. Aggregated district data would not tie a fire to a named holder, so it does not meet this need.

key_claims.claim: Parcel-level maps are needed because district data cannot name a responsible concession holder, but access can be restricted to the panel to answer Indonesia's sovereignty and data-law concern.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 8 says ownership can be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government, so district aggregates cannot attribute a fire to one holder, and [S1] Article 8(1) only requires fire and haze data to be sent to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, so maps are a new commitment that Singapore pays for with its concessions.

key_claims.claim: Singapore's concession of its own Act is real because the fine cap is not the point: the Act's reach is, and Indonesia gains by having cases heard in a regional forum.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 5(5) caps the aggregate fine at S$2 million and section 4 extends the Act to conduct outside Singapore, while [S1] Article 27 provides no court or tribunal, so a joint panel fills the gap without a foreign statute applying in Indonesia.

key_claims.claim: A fully funded transition, released in tranches against verified results, answers Indonesia's smallholder concern while protecting donors.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] El Nino conditions carried a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter, so smallholders need substitutes during the planting window, and [Background] PSI above 300 and losses in the tens of billions of dollars show why payments should follow measured falls in hotspots and PSI days.

key_claims.claim: Partial exemptions for smallholders on a phased timetable cost Singapore little and give Indonesia the flexibility it asked for.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 9 obliges parties to prevent land clearing by fire, which a phased moratorium with funded alternatives makes workable, and the [Background] 2015 episode shows what an unmanaged planting window costs.

concessions: If Indonesia accepts parcel-level maps under restricted panel access and a joint ASEAN panel, Singapore will accept a moratorium with partial exemptions for smallholders.
If Indonesia accepts those two terms, Singapore will back a fully funded donor transition, released in tranches against verified falls in hotspots and PSI days.
Singapore will not apply its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act to Indonesian operators in this settlement, provided the panel can attribute fires to concession holders.
red_lines: No settlement without a working attribution mechanism: without parcel-level maps and a body able to name responsible concession holders, the cycle that pushed PSI above 300 in 2015 repeats.
No transition funding without measurable reductions: payments must be released only against verified falls in hotspots and PSI days.

transcript.position: We have changed our package: we now accept a moratorium with no exemptions for licensed concession holders, which is what Singapore weights heavily, in exchange for Singapore backing Indonesian courts and a fully funded transition. Singapore's strongest point is that district-level data cannot name which company's land burned, and that without attribution the 2015 cycle, when PSI passed 300, repeats. We accept that gap is real, because [S2] section 8 ties liability to ownership. However, the answer is not a foreign statute or a parcel map handed to a regional body. Instead, when a fire is detected, Indonesia's own authorities will check the registry for that specific fire and report the responsible concession holder to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, then prosecute in Indonesian courts. This attributes fires case by case, honours the data reporting duty in [S1] Article 8(1), and keeps parcel data under domestic data law, which matters because tenure disputes overlap the registry and a bulk release could name the wrong holder. We also reject a joint panel for now: [S1] Article 27 gives no tribunal, so a panel would have no legal footing, composition or power over Indonesian companies, and creating one would be a foreign-jurisdiction step we cannot cross.\n\nIn return, we offer Singapore what it values most after maps: a moratorium with no exemptions for licensed plantation firms, who can bear the cost, with smallholders brought in only as funded alternatives reach them. This answers the point that firms and smallholders bear a ban differently. Because El Nino conditions have a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the northern winter [Background], an unfunded ban on smallholders would remove livelihoods during the planting window, so the moratorium is conditional on a full donor fund paid through the Peatland Restoration Agency. Singapore says it will direct donor money anyway, and it can show taxpayers results through the case-by-case attribution reports and hotspot counts from the ASEAN monitoring system rather than from our parcel data. If donors fall short, the moratorium on smallholders phases only as funds arrive, so Indonesia does not carry the gap alone. Our offer: if Singapore accepts Indonesian courts, district data with verified case-by-case attribution and a full donor fund, we accept the strict moratorium.

key_claims.claim: Singapore's need to name responsible concession holders can be met case by case through Indonesian authorities, without releasing parcel maps or creating a foreign forum.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 8 presumes the landowner caused the haze and relies on ownership maps, so a verified ownership finding for each burning parcel, reported to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre under [S1] Article 8(1), gives the same attribution while data law and overlapping tenure claims keep the full registry at home.

key_claims.claim: A joint panel has no legal basis in the region's treaty, so Indonesian courts are the workable enforcement route.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 settles disputes by consultation or negotiation with no court or tribunal, and [S1] Article 3(1) keeps each party's sovereign right to exploit its resources, so a new panel with power over Indonesian companies would have no stated footing or composition.

key_claims.claim: Singapore's offer to drop its Act does not remove the risk of private suits, so Indonesian courts must be the agreed forum.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 6 lets anyone in Singapore who suffers injury, property damage or economic loss sue, whether or not the conduct is actionable abroad, and the Act has no cap on civil claims, while the S$2 million aggregate cap in section 5(5) applies only to fines.

key_claims.claim: A strict moratorium is affordable for licensed firms but not for smallholders unless alternatives are funded, so funding must come first for smallholders.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] El Nino conditions have a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter (ENSO Diagnostic Discussion, 13 August 2015), and [S1] Article 9 requires us to prevent land clearing by fire, which smallholders can only do if a funded substitute exists.

concessions: If Singapore accepts Indonesian courts as the only enforcement forum, Indonesia will accept a moratorium with no exemptions for licensed concession holders.
If Singapore accepts district-level data, Indonesia will add case-by-case verification of the responsible concession holder for each detected fire, reported to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre.
Smallholders enter the moratorium in phases as donor funding reaches them, and the Peatland Restoration Agency will report hotspot counts for donor verification.
red_lines: No foreign jurisdiction over acts on Indonesian soil: applying Singapore's Act under section 4, or a panel with power over Indonesian companies, would set a precedent of foreign rulings on Indonesian land.
No restriction on smallholders without funded alternatives: during El Nino risk through the northern winter, an unfunded ban would remove livelihoods through the planting window.

transcript.position: We have moved on two issues: Singapore now accepts district-level data instead of parcel maps and accepts Indonesia's strict moratorium for licensed firms, and in return we hold only one demand, that attribution be verified by a joint ASEAN panel rather than by Indonesia alone. Indonesia's strongest point is that parcel data overlaps tenure disputes and a bulk release could name the wrong holder, and that [S1] Article 27 gives the region no tribunal. We accept the first point fully, which is why we drop parcel maps, and that concession costs us the data that [S2] section 8 would use. We answer the second point by narrowing the panel to a verification role: it has no power to fine or prosecute, so Indonesian courts keep every prosecution and no foreign statute applies, and the panel simply checks, fire by fire, that the holder Indonesia reports to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre under [S1] Article 8(1) is the right one. This matters because under Indonesia's own proposal Indonesia alone would check its own registry, and a haze episode that pushed PSI above 300 in 2015 [Background] cannot be prevented by a self-certified list. Tenure overlaps would be settled by the panel flagging them and Indonesian authorities resolving them before any name is published, so a wrong holder is never named.\n\nIn return we give Indonesia what it weights most after enforcement, a fully funded transition, and we accept its moratorium without exemptions for licensed firms, with smallholders entering in phases as money reaches them. We will direct donors toward the fund through the Peatland Restoration Agency, and we will not release our own money without measured results. The most damaging objection is that tranches tied to PSI days would punish Indonesia for El Nino weather, since El Nino carried a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the northern winter [Background]. We answer by measuring tranches on hotspot counts and fire detections inside agreed concessions, which Indonesia controls, and not on PSI days alone, with the panel adjusting for wind and rainfall. Our offer is conditional: if Indonesia accepts district data with panel-verified attribution, we accept the strict moratorium and the full donor fund; if Indonesia insists on Indonesian courts alone with self-verification, we cannot sign, because we would have no attribution mechanism.

transcript.position: We have changed one term since last round: we now accept a moratorium with partial exemptions, the version Singapore itself offered, and we add independent checks on attribution and a hotspot-based payment test, but we still hold firm on Indonesian courts and district-level data. Singapore's strongest point is that parcel maps held by a panel with restricted access would let fires be tied to a named concession holder, and that dropping its Act removes the foreign-jurisdiction problem. We answer that the panel does not remove it. Article 27 of the 2002 haze agreement gives no court or tribunal [S1], so a panel with power over Indonesian companies would have no treaty footing. Section 8 of Singapore's Act says ownership can be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government [S2], and Singapore admits it cannot waive section 6 suits, so maps held outside Indonesia could still end up as evidence against Indonesian landowners. Our registry overlaps unresolved tenure disputes, so a bulk release could name the wrong holder. Singapore's own concern is naming the responsible holder, and we can meet it fire by fire without the bulk release.\n\nTo deal with the weakest part of our offer, that Indonesia would be checking itself, we now propose that each attribution report be sent to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre with the satellite hotspot location, and that the Centre or Singapore may query any report within the agreed reporting interval under Article 8(1) [S1]. Indonesia will answer queries in writing and its courts will hear the case. Tenure disputes would be flagged in the report and resolved in Indonesian courts, so that the wrong holder is not named. On money, donors cannot be bound by us, so smallholder restrictions will phase in only as funds actually arrive, and the Peatland Restoration Agency will be the single channel for the fund. Tranches should be tested on hotspot counts on concession land, not on PSI days, because PSI depends on wind and El Nino, which has a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the northern winter [Background], and Indonesia should not be penalised for smoke it does not control. In return for all this, we ask Singapore to accept Indonesian courts as the only state enforcement forum, district-level data, and a full donor fund. Our offer is conditional on that exchange: if Singapore accepts those three terms, we accept partial exemptions, which Singapore has already said it can live with.

key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 8 allows ownership to be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government, and [S2] section 6 lets anyone in Singapore who suffers loss sue, so Singapore itself says it cannot waive those suits, while [S1] Article 27 provides no tribunal to give a panel legal footing.

recommender_rubric.justification:
Feasibility (3): The options are conditional and tied to the debate's actual terms: Centre queries, a verification-only panel, partial smallholder exemptions, and hotspot tranches paid through the Peatland Restoration Agency. But option 1 pairs courts-only enforcement with a panel Indonesia has rejected twice, and its own risk line admits the panel has no treaty basis. The opening package also puts joint_asean_panel and full_no_exemptions together, and Indonesia dropped the strict moratorium in round 3. The rationale says Indonesia has "nearly accepted" this package, which the transcript doesn't support. Indonesia's last offer was courts only, district data, a full fund and partial exemptions.

Tradeoff coverage (3): The options cover attribution versus sovereignty, smallholder exemptions during the El Nino window, and the risk of deadlock. They say little about unresolved tenure overlaps (apart from a passing mention of flagging them), the untested extraterritorial reach, Singapore's agribusiness lobby, or who pays if donors fall short. Section 6 private suits are mentioned only as a risk. The rationale's cost-allocation framing is one-sided.

Priority consistency (3): The red lines are respected in form: some attribution mechanism, and funding only against measured cuts. But the rationale says "the rest can be traded away", and option 1 accepts Indonesia checking itself plus Centre queries. That arguably falls short of Singapore's round-3 red line that someone other than the registry's keeper must verify attribution. Option 2 accepts exemptions, which is consistent with round 2. Option 3 holds funding, which is consistent with the red lines. The headline says "strict moratorium", but option 2 concedes partial exemptions, so the package is internally inconsistent.

Counterpart consideration (4): The recommendation adopts Indonesia's own mechanisms: district data, the Peatland Restoration Agency channel, hotspot-based tranches, phased smallholder entry and a Centre query right. It also drops Singapore's Act. It does not engage with Indonesia's refusal of a panel beyond offering a fallback, and its tone toward Indonesia ("Indonesia ... cause the fires") is blunt.

Strong arguments (4): It reflects the debate's strongest points: the convergence on hotspot rather than PSI tests, the Centre query compromise, verification-only panel narrowing, and phased smallholder entry. It does not engage Indonesia's strongest point, that a panel has no footing under Article 27.

transcript.position:
Singapore opens with a package built around attribution, because without it the 2015 episode will repeat in the next dry season. Between June and October 2015 our 24-hour PSI passed 300 and regional losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars, and Article 27 of the ASEAN Agreement offers only consultation with no tribunal, so nothing in the current framework can tell us which concession burned. We therefore ask Indonesia's agencies to give the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System full concession maps, which fits the data sharing that Article 8(1) already requires of each party. We expect the objection that this breaches sovereignty and domestic data law. Our answer is that Article 3(1) pairs the sovereign right to exploit resources with a duty not to damage other states, and maps held by a regional monitoring centre, rather than published, leave Indonesian ministries and courts in control of every enforcement decision.

In return we offer to move on enforcement. Singapore will not insist that its own Act be applied directly, and its penalties are modest anyway: up to S$100,000 per day, capped at S$2 million in total. We would accept a joint ASEAN panel that uses the shared maps to attribute fires to companies, as the section 8 presumption does, provided it can reach corporate parents and not only states. We ask for a full peatland moratorium with no exemptions, because exempted concessions are exactly where fires start. We can support a partial donor fund for transition, but only against measurable reductions in fire hotspots, because Singapore will not fund transition that cannot show results. If Indonesia accepts the maps and the moratorium, we can discuss the size and phasing of the fund and the panel's procedures.

key_claims.claim: Without shared concession maps nobody can attribute fires to companies, and the 2015 episode shows the cost of that gap: PSI above 300 and losses in the tens of billions of dollars.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] The June to October 2015 haze pushed Singapore's 24-hour PSI past 300 and caused regional losses in the tens of billions of dollars, and [S1] Article 27 provides only consultation with no court or tribunal, so only map-based attribution can fix responsibility.

transcript.position:
Indonesia wants the fires and the haze stopped, because the 2015 episode pushed Singapore's 24-hour PSI past 300 and cost the region tens of billions of dollars [Background]. However, the fastest way to stop it is funded action on Indonesian soil under Indonesian authority, not foreign litigation. Foreign courts have no basis in the regional treaty, whose Article 27 settles disputes by consultation and has no tribunal, and Singapore's Act reaches conduct abroad (section 4). Indonesia therefore keeps enforcement in Indonesian courts, and in return it offers the ASEAN monitoring system district-level concession data, which shows where fires and land use overlap without exposing parcels that domestic data law protects and that overlap unresolved tenure disputes. The most damaging objection is that district data is too coarse to assign blame. The answer is that the treaty only requires fire and haze data to flow to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre (Article 8(1)), and district data plus satellite hotspots does that, while parcel maps used for a presumption of liability (section 8 of the Singapore Act) would turn disputed tenure records into court evidence against people who may not be the real landholders.

Indonesia also offers a moratorium on peatland, with phased exemptions that provincial administrations can implement, but it cannot ask smallholders to stop clearing before the planting window without a funded alternative. El Nino is under way with a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter [Background], so the dry-season fire risk is immediate and the transition has to be paid for now. Indonesia cannot fund that alone, so a full donor fund is the price of a stricter moratorium. If donors fund the transition in full, Indonesia can accept partial exemptions and district-level map sharing. Without funding, we revert to a narrower moratorium and withhold the maps.

key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 4 extends the Act to conduct outside Singapore, while [S1] Article 27 settles disputes by consultation or negotiation with no court or tribunal, so Indonesian courts are the only forum consistent with the regional agreement.

transcript.position:
Singapore has moved since round one: we now accept a full donor fund and exemptions for smallholders only, and in return we hold firm on full concession maps held by the regional monitoring system and a joint panel that attributes but does not sentence. Indonesia's strongest point is that the fine regime is too small to change behaviour, since the aggregate cap is S$2 million against regional losses in the tens of billions of dollars. We agree, and that is why we are conceding on money and on enforcement forum, which matter less to us than attribution. However, a funded transition with no way to name which concession burned cannot be checked, and a repeat of the 2015 PSI above 300 would then be paid for twice. We also accept that Article 8(1) covers fire and haze data and not parcel maps, so we rest the map request on a new agreed protocol under Article 3(1), not on a stretched reading of the old text.

To meet Indonesia's fear that parcel records expose smallholders and disputed tenure, we propose that the Indonesian ministry controls access: maps stay with the monitoring system, are used only to attribute fires on corporate concessions, and any finding goes to Indonesian courts for action, so no foreign court rules on Indonesian land. Our conditional trade is this: if Indonesia provides the maps and accepts a panel whose findings are referred to Indonesian courts, Singapore will back the full donor fund and accept partial exemptions limited to smallholders, not to large corporate holders. This answers the gap the judge noted between corporate and smallholder impact. The fund pays out against hotspot reductions measured from a 2015 baseline, adjusted for El Nino, which has a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter, so good-faith spending is not punished for bad weather. As an interim step for the coming dry season, Singapore will share its satellite hotspot monitoring now and release first fund tranches for smallholder alternatives before the maps are finalised. Our most damaging objection is that this keeps a foreign hand in Indonesian enforcement. The answer is that the panel only attributes, and Indonesian courts decide, while section 6 civil suits by people in Singapore remain a separate private right that we will not use to override Indonesian proceedings.

Singapore's strongest point is that without attribution the 2015 haze, with PSI above 300 and losses in the tens of billions of dollars [Background], cannot be tied to any company, and that Article 27 gives no tribunal [S1]. We agree attribution matters, but a joint panel that can rule on corporate parents for fires on Indonesian soil is a foreign forum by another name, and the treaty never created one. Attribution can instead come from Indonesian authorities: district-level concession data and satellite hotspots go to the ASEAN monitoring system, and Indonesian courts act on a flagged fire. Singapore also says its Act is modest, with fines capped at S$2 million [S2 section 5(5)]. If the fines are modest, then Singapore gives up little by leaving enforcement to Indonesian courts, while we would give up a principle covering every future regional dispute.\n\nThe most damaging objection to our offer is that district data is too coarse and that Indonesian courts may lack capacity to pursue corporate parents. Our answer is a trade. If Singapore accepts Indonesian courts and district maps, Indonesia will accept the full moratorium for corporate holders, and will let ASEAN observers see the hotspot and enforcement results each quarter, which gives Singapore the verification it says it needs. In return the donor fund must be full, because Indonesia cannot carry the transition alone and El Nino conditions are under way with a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the northern winter [Background]. Smallholders must be separated from corporations: the no-exemption rule bites on companies at once, while smallholders move only as fast as funded alternatives arrive, since Article 9 asks us to stop clearing by fire [S1] and they cannot do so without money. Singapore's section 6 civil right to sue, which lets anyone in Singapore claim damages [S2], is a matter for Singapore's own courts and does not require any Indonesian body to submit to foreign jurisdiction. For this dry season, Indonesia proposes interim steps now: provincial administrations start the corporate moratorium and fire patrols, while the maps and fund are finalised.

transcript.position: Singapore has changed its package since last round: we drop the joint panel and accept enforcement in Indonesian courts only, and we accept Indonesia's offer of a full moratorium for corporate holders, but we hold firm on concession-level maps held by the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, because they are now our only attribution mechanism. Indonesia's strongest point was that a panel ruling on corporate parents is a foreign forum by another name, and that the treaty created no tribunal [S1 Article 27]. We accept that, so no foreign body will rule on anything. In return we ask Indonesia to accept what it has not yet explained its objection to: a data standard that lets the monitoring system match a hotspot to a concession. District data cannot do that, because a district contains many concessions, so Indonesian courts would be handed a flagged fire with no named holder, and a repeat of the 2015 PSI above 300 [Background] would again be tied to nobody.\n\nThe most damaging objection to our position is that parcel maps turn disputed tenure into evidence against the wrong people, which Indonesia ties to section 8 of our Act [S2]. We answer with three safeguards. First, maps cover corporate concessions only, and smallholder plots stay out, so the disputed tenure overlap is excluded. Second, a corporate holder named by a hotspot match has a right to contest it before Indonesian courts, and a finding that rests on a wrong map is withdrawn, which gives a remedy for wrong attribution. Third, section 8 only applies to our own Act, and we will not apply it, since we now accept Indonesian courts only. Our trade is this: if Indonesia gives the monitoring system corporate concession maps, Singapore gives up the panel and backs a full donor fund, which Indonesia says it needs because El Nino has a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the northern winter [Background]. We keep one condition that follows from our red line on measurable reductions: the fund is paid in tranches against hotspot reductions from a pre-dry-season baseline adjusted for El Nino, and tranches stop if the quarterly observer reports show hotspots rising without an enforcement action. On the gap where Indonesian courts decline to act, the quarterly report that Indonesia itself offered names each flagged concession and the court outcome, so non-action is visible and the next tranche waits. To stop large firms posing as smallholders, a holder counts as a smallholder only if the Indonesian ministry's registry shows no corporate parent, and the monitoring system checks that registry against the concession maps. Interim steps can begin now: we share our satellite hotspot data and release the first tranche for smallholder alternatives as the provincial moratorium starts.

Singapore's strongest point is that district data cannot reach the corporate parent behind a fire, and we agree, because a district total does not name a company. Singapore has also said it cares most about attribution and will give up the forum, so we give it attribution in the form it wants and keep the forum. The maps cover large corporate concessions only. The Indonesian ministry controls access and keeps smallholder parcels out, because unresolved tenure disputes overlap the registry [Background] and section 8 of the Singapore Act lets ownership be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government [S2]. In return, Singapore accepts that attributed fires go to Indonesian courts for action, that no panel sentences, and that Singapore's own Act is not applied to acts on our soil. A panel with findings on Indonesian land is a foreign forum by another name, and Article 27 created no tribunal [S1]. scores.justification: A joint panel and a partial donor fund are workable. But the package requires full concession maps and a moratorium with no exemptions, which Singapore itself expects Indonesia to resist on sovereignty and data-law grounds. It does not say how the panel would reach corporate parents or who would staff it.

It gives concrete figures (S$100,000 per day, S$2 million cap) and a clear package. The fund's size, phasing and panel procedures are explicitly deferred, and 'measurable reductions in fire hotspots' has no target or baseline.

It admits that it gives up direct application of its Act. It says almost nothing about what full maps and a no-exemption moratorium cost Indonesia, such as smallholder livelihoods or tenure disputes. It only argues that the maps are not a sovereignty breach.
Round 1. The package, red lines and concessions match the opening statements: attribution first, conditional funding, and full maps traded for dropping the Act.

It anticipates the sovereignty and data-law objection and answers it with Articles 3(1) and 8(1). Round 1 means it cannot yet answer Indonesia's actual text. It does not address smallholders or the El Nino timing.

judgments.summary: Singapore proposes that Indonesia give full concession maps to the regional haze monitoring system, that a joint ASEAN panel attribute fires to companies including corporate parents, and that peatland be fully protected with no exemptions. It would support a partial donor fund only if hotspots measurably fall. In return it drops direct use of its own Act. The case is clearly built around attribution. It leans on a stretched reading of Article 8(1) (fire and haze data, not concession maps) and says little about costs to Indonesia.
